conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **EPDS**—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—which looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the past week. Your answers stay between you and your care team, and there’s no “right” or “wrong” response; we just want to understand how best to support you. It’s ten questions, asked conversationally, and should only take a few minutes. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

I’ve still been able to laugh—like, my partner did something silly yesterday and I caught myself giggling. It maybe takes a second longer to feel it than before I had the baby, but the joy is definitely there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that’s pretty much how I’d put it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to things—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings dinner. They’re small, but they still feel nice.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I figure it’s just part of the newborn phase—not something I’m doing wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay when she’s napping, even though I can see her chest moving. It only lasts a minute and I can brush it off, but it pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not panicky—just that quick jolt of worry when I check on her breathing. It’s gone in seconds and I can settle myself pretty easily.
Things have been getting on top of me
A couple of times, sure—like yesterday when she wouldn’t nap and the laundry was piling up, I felt a bit swamped. Once my partner got home and held her so I could shower, it passed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—when the baby goes down for a three-hour stretch, I can fall right back to sleep myself.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t say miserable—maybe a little teary once or twice when I’m extra tired, but it lifts quickly and I’m back to feeling okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried at all this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all.

You shared that laughter still comes easily, small daily pleasures like coffee and your mom's dinners bring genuine enjoyment, and you can soothe yourself when brief worries pop up. Occasional moments of feeling swamped resolve quickly with a partner's help, and you have not experienced persistent sadness, sleep disruption beyond normal newborn hours, or thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes sudden, intrusive worries about the baby's breathing that appear without cause and are hard to control, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes occasional overwhelm ('a couple of times...felt a bit swamped') but also notes quick recovery with support, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 7 falls below the 8-point threshold where postpartum depression becomes more likely. You endorsed only mild, situational <sym>anxiety</sym> and brief <sym>mood dips</sym> that remit with support, not meeting the two-week duration or five-symptom minimum required by <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. <quote>I can brush it off</quote> and <quote>it lifts quickly</quote> indicate retained coping capacity. No safety concerns were elicited. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum follow-up and re-screen if mood, anxiety, or coping worsen
2. Encourage consistent partner or family breaks to curb overwhelm
3. Practice quick grounding techniques (slow breathing, sensory focus) when sudden worries arise
4. Maintain good sleep hygiene: nap when baby naps, limit screens before rest periods
5. Reach out promptly if sadness, panic, guilt, or self-harm thoughts increase
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum parent, ≤ 6 wk post-delivery (perinatal visit)  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed  
• Transient, situational worry about infant breathing (Q4/5) – no persistent panic  
• Occasional tearfulness when fatigued (Q8) – mood recovers quickly  
• Brief feeling “swamped” with household tasks; resolves with partner support (Q6)

Symptoms denied  
Loss of pleasure, pervasive guilt, sleep disruption beyond infant demands, crying spells, suicidal ideation.

Pattern  
Mood remains generally positive; retains capacity for enjoyment and self-soothing. Stress reactions are mild, situation-specific, and remit with practical help.

Screening significance  
Current responses do not indicate high-risk postpartum depression or anxiety. No safety concerns elicited. Continue routine postpartum follow-up; re-screen if mood, anxiety, or coping deteriorates.
